name: Signbook
powers: Formulas and signs for 'signing' wounds, bleeding, illness, and fire.
description: A signbook (signeringsbok), a hand-copied Swedish book of signs used by folk healers and 'kloka gummor', the wise women and men of the parish. The volumes collected prayers, magical signs, and formulae for 'signing' wounds, bleeding, disease, and fire. Several Swedish signbooks from the 17th to 19th centuries survive in archives, mixing Christian prayers with folk-magical practice.
source: Swedish folk-medicine collections (e.g. Nordiska museet, Riksarkivet)

name: Rune Calendar
powers: Read like a perpetual printed almanac of the church year.
description: A rune calendar (runkalender or runstav), a perpetual almanac carved on a long wooden or horn staff, used in Sweden from the Middle Ages into the nineteenth century. Each year's structure was fixed with runes: one rune row marked the weekdays, another the golden numbers that place the movable feasts. The staff was read like a printed calendar and was long carried by Swedish farmers and seafarers.
source: Museum collections of rune calendars (e.g. Nordiska museet)

name: Troll Porridge Bowl
powers: Appeases the tomte so the farm prospers.
description: At Christmas, Swedish farm families set out a bowl of rice porridge with butter for the tomte, the farm's household spirit. The bowl was left in the attic, the barn, or by the hearth; if the butter was hidden or the porridge forgotten, the tomte was said to abandon the farm or work mischief. The custom, documented across Sweden into the twentieth century, is the subject of many tomte tales.
source: Swedish Christmas custom and tomte tales

name: The Magic Churn
powers: Dairy magic that brings or steals the butter.
description: A butter churn that witches were believed to bewitch or to work from afar. In Swedish folk belief a witch (trollkona) could send a 'mjölkhare', a butter or cream hare, to steal milk from neighbours' cows and churns, or charm a churn so that butter would not come. Counter-magic included heating a knife in the fire and running it through the churn to break the spell.
source: Swedish folk belief about milk and butter magic

name: Witch Broom
material: Birch twigs bound to a handle
powers: Carries the rider to the witches' sabbath mountain Blåkulla.
description: The broom (kvast) that, in Swedish folk belief, carried witches to Blåkulla, the witches' sabbath mountain, especially on Maundy Thursday before Easter. The 'påskkärring', the Easter witch, was thought to ride a broom, or a cow, goat, or pitchfork, to Blåkulla. People blocked chimneys and hid brooms behind stoves to stop the flights, and the belief shaped Sweden's Easter-witch custom.
source: Swedish belief in the Easter witches of Blåkulla

name: Knotted Rope Charm
maker: Tied by a 'wise' seller or Sami sorcerer
powers: Untying a knot raises wind; the third knot calls a storm.
description: A rope or cord with three knots, tied by a 'wise' seller and sold to sailors as a wind charm. Untying the first knot raised a gentle wind, the second a stronger breeze, and the third a storm, so prudent captains kept the third knot tied. The three-knotted wind cord is documented in Nordic and Sami maritime folklore and was often credited to Lapp (Sami) sorcery.
source: Nordic maritime folklore on wind magic

name: The Church Bell Against Storms
powers: Its ringing breaks up storms, drives away evil, and helps stop fires.
description: Swedish church bells were believed to protect the parish: they were rung to break up thunderclouds, drive away storms and pestilence, and even to help stop fires. The casting of a new bell was accompanied by rites, and the bells were thought to carry a blessing that evil powers could not withstand. Ringing against bad weather ('ringning mot oväder') is recorded in many Swedish parishes.
source: Swedish parish tradition of bell ringing against the weather

name: The Magic Scythe
maker: Given as a wonder-gift in the tale
powers: Mows grain by itself, without a hand to swing it.
description: A scythe in Swedish folktales that cuts grain by itself, without a hand to swing it. In the tale of the magic scythe, the wonderful tool performs the harvest work of many men, sparing its owner the labour of mowing. The self-working scythe belongs to a family of Swedish wonder-tools in which ordinary farm implements act on their own.
source: Swedish folktale 'The Magic Scythe'

name: Silver Buckles
description: Silver buckles and clasps worn with Swedish regional folk dress, on belts, shoes, and collars. Such silver, often inherited and re-used across generations, was engraved with initials and dates and served as both ornament and stored wealth. Wealthy folk wore heavy rectangular 'spännen'; poorer folk wore simpler clasps. The buckles are a documented part of the folk-costume tradition.
source: Swedish folk-costume and silver traditions

name: Bridal Crown
powers: Marks the bride as a crowned bride, bringing honour to the wedding.
description: The bridal crown (brudkrona), a crown of gilt silver or brass that Swedish churches owned and lent to brides for the wedding ceremony. The custom, recorded from the Middle Ages, made the bride a 'crowned bride' and the crown a symbol of honour and virginity. Rules sometimes required a fee, and the crown was kept locked in the church between weddings.
source: Swedish church custom of the bridal crown

name: Swedish Folk Costume
material: Wool and linen with silver and embroidery
description: The Swedish folk costume (folkdräkt), the regional dress of parish and province, worn for work and festivals and gradually codified from the 18th century. Each district had its own colours, cut, embroidery, and accessories such as the flounced apron and the bodice. The national costume, the Sverigedräkt, was created in 1903 by Märta Jörgensen and has since been widely adopted.
source: Swedish folk-dress research (e.g. Nordiska museet)

name: The Ljungby Horn
maker: Said to have belonged to a troll
powers: Drinking horn of the troll folk, kept in the church at Ljungby.
description: A horn at the centre of a legend from Ljungby in Småland. A troll who joined a wedding dance was said to have left behind his great drinking horn, which was then kept in the local church; whoever drank from it was cured or grew a beard, according to the variant. The horn is linked in tradition to the troll's magic, and its story is told together with the companion pipe.
source: Småland legend of the Ljungby horn and pipe

name: The Ljungby Pipe
maker: Said to have belonged to a troll
powers: Blowing it was said to set people dancing against their will.
description: The pipe that a troll was said to have left at Ljungby in Småland together with his horn. In the legend the pipe, like the horn, was kept by the parish and remembered as a possession of the troll folk; blowing it was sometimes said to make people dance against their will. The horn and pipe together form one of Sweden's best-known legends of a troll at a human feast.
source: Småland legend of the Ljungby horn and pipe

name: The Magic Table
aliases: Table, the Ass and the Stick
maker: Given as a wonder-gift in the tales
powers: Sets itself with food and drink at a word.
description: A table that sets itself with food, a recurring wonder-object of Swedish folk tales. At a word the self-serving table covers itself with dishes and ale, so the hero never goes hungry; the motif usually appears in tales where a magic object is given as a reward and later stolen and replaced with a worthless copy. It belongs to the family of self-working marvels in Swedish wonder-tales.
source: Swedish wonder-tale motif of the self-setting table

name: The Golden Keys
powers: Unlock doors and rewards for the hero who wins them.
description: Golden keys that appear in a Swedish folk tale, unlocking a reward or a forbidden treasure for the hero who obtains them. The keys belong to the tale's wonder-logic: ordinary locks fall open before them, and possession of the keys brings the hero to fortune. The motif is told as part of the tale 'The Golden Keys'.
source: Swedish folktale 'The Golden Keys'

name: The Queen's Necklace
maker: Court jewel, object of the tale
description: A necklace in a Swedish folk tale, worn by a queen and central to the story's test or reward. In the tale 'The Queen's Necklace', the necklace passes through the hands of the characters and its loss, theft, or recovery drives the plot. The jewel is a typical treasure of wonder-tales, standing for wealth, rank, and the queen's honour.
source: Swedish folktale 'The Queen's Necklace'

name: The Skin Satchel
maker: Sewn for a magical purpose in the tale
powers: Holds an impossible store or releases the tale's marvels.
description: A satchel made of animal skin that carries magic in a Swedish folk tale. In the tale 'The Skin Satchel', the humble leather bag turns out to hold an impossible store, or to have been sewn for a magical purpose, and its opening releases the story's marvels. The satchel is one of many everyday objects in Swedish wonder-tales that conceal power.
source: Swedish folktale 'The Skin Satchel'

name: The Magician's Cape
maker: Worn by the magician of the tale
powers: Lets the wearer fly, turn invisible, or work spells.
description: A cape that gives its wearer magical power in a Swedish folk tale. In the tale 'The Magician's Cape', the cloak lets the hero fly, become invisible, or work spells, and is won, lost, and recovered through the story's tests. The cape is a classic object of wonder-tales: a garment of ordinary cut that carries extraordinary ability.
source: Swedish folktale 'The Magician's Cape'

name: The Barrel Bung
powers: Conjures food, drink, or gold for its owner.
description: A barrel bung, the wooden stopper of a cask, that works magic in a Swedish folk tale. In the tale 'The Barrel Bung', the small wooden plug proves able to conjure food, drink, or gold for its owner. It is one of the many humble objects that Swedish wonder-tales turn into providers of plenty.
source: Swedish folktale 'The Barrel Bung'

name: Nyckelharpa
maker: Swedish instrument makers, especially in Uppland
description: The keyed fiddle (nyckelharpa), a bowed string instrument with keys that stop the strings, played in Swedish folk music since the 16th century and especially associated with Uppland. Its buzzing drone strings and chromatic key rows give it its characteristic sound. It was revived in the early 20th century and remains a national instrument, played at dance and fest.
source: Swedish instrument history and folk-music research

name: Dala Horse
maker: Carvers of the Mora region, Dalarna
description: The Dala horse (Dalahäst), the carved wooden horse of Dalarna, painted in red, white, blue, and green with a floral saddle. The craft grew from toys carved during long winter evenings in the 17th century into a famous local industry around Mora, where the horses are still hand-carved and painted. The Dala horse has become the best-known symbol of Swedish craft.
source: Dalarna woodcarving tradition (Mora)

name: Midsummer Maypole
maker: Raised by the village at Midsummer
powers: Centre of the Midsummer dance and fertility rites.
description: The midsummer pole (midsommarstång or majstång), a tall pole decorated with greenery, flowers, and rings, raised on Midsummer Eve and danced around in Swedish tradition. Songs, ring-dances, and games circle the pole, and the custom is recorded in Sweden from the 17th century. The pole is central to the Midsummer celebration and its bonfire-night rites.
source: Swedish Midsummer tradition

name: Yule Goat
description: The Yule goat (julbock), a goat figure of straw bound with red ribbon, made in Sweden at Christmas. The straw goat descends from older beliefs around Thor's goats and the 'julbock' who once brought the Christmas gifts before the tree took the role. Today the most famous example is the giant Gävle goat, erected and burned each December.
source: Swedish Christmas tradition of the julbock

name: The Troll's Mitten
description: A mitten that a troll or giant is said to have dropped and left behind, so large that a human could use it for shelter or sleep inside the thumb. The motif of the lost glove or mitten of the troll folk appears in Swedish tales as proof of the hidden people's size, and finding it is both marvellous and dangerous.
source: Swedish troll-tale motif of the lost mitten

name: The Bewitched Knife
powers: Steel laid across the cradle keeps the changeling away; a knife breaks spells.
description: An iron knife that Swedish folk tradition used against harmful magic. A knife or other steel laid across a newborn's cradle was believed to keep the bortbyting, the changeling, from swapping the child, and a knife was also run through a bewitched churn or struck into the threshold to break spells. The sign-carved knife also served the healer in 'signing' rites.
source: Swedish folk belief in steel against harmful magic

name: The Offer Stone
powers: Cups held offerings for blessing and healing.
description: The offer stone (offersten), a boulder with cup-shaped hollows where offerings were made. Hundreds of such stones survive across Sweden, often beside churches, springs, or old cult sites; small gifts of coins, food, or tar were placed in the cups, and in later Christian times the stones were avoided or 'baptised'. The cup-marked stones are counted among Sweden's oldest cult objects.
source: Swedish antiquarian and ethnological records of offer stones

name: The Holy Spring
maker: Natural spring, named for a saint
powers: Healing water for the sick who visit on the appointed day.
description: The holy spring (heliga källan), a spring or well that Swedish folk tradition credited with healing. Such springs, often named for a saint, were visited for cures on particular days; pilgrims left offerings of coins, linen, or crosses, and some springs were said to swell or glow before miracles. Many Swedish holy springs became pilgrimage sites that the church later absorbed or closed.
source: Swedish holy-spring tradition and place-name studies

name: The Kettle of the Underjordiska
powers: Returned filled with gold, or borrowed at a price.
description: A pot or kettle that the underjordiska, the hidden people beneath the earth, were said to borrow from farm households. In Swedish legend a woman lends a kettle to the hidden folk and finds it returned filled with gold or a gift, or learns that borrowing from them carries its own price. The borrowed kettle is a common motif in stories of the underjordiska.
source: Swedish legends of the underjordiska

name: The Troll Shoes
maker: Worn by a troll in the tale
powers: Let the wearer stride over mountains or move faster than thought.
description: Shoes worn by a troll in a Swedish folk tale. In the tale 'The Troll Shoes', the troll's footwear, or the wearing of it, lets a human stride over mountains or move faster than thought, and the shoes are won or put on during the tale's test. The troll's shoes are a typical wonder-object of Swedish troll tales.
source: Swedish folktale 'The Troll Shoes'

name: The Golden Cradle
description: A cradle of gold in a Swedish folk tale, in which a special child is laid and around which the tale's wonder unfolds. In 'The Golden Cradle', the precious cradle marks the child's destiny and the family's fortune, and its making or finding drives the story. The golden cradle is an emblem of the wonder-tale's promise of wealth and favour.
source: Swedish folktale 'The Golden Cradle'

name: The Flower of Happiness
maker: Grows at Sunnymount Crest in the tale
powers: Possessing it was said to bring happiness.
description: The flower of happiness, the marvel of a tale told at Sunnymount Crest: a flower whose possession, or whose bloom, was said to bring happiness to whoever found it. In the tale the search for the flower tests the seeker, and the happiness it brings is measured in the finding. The flower is an object-lesson of the wonder-tale rather than a real plant.
source: Swedish folktale 'The Flower of Happiness'

name: The Cat of Norrhult
description: A bewitched cat in a folk tale from Norrhult in Småland. In the tale 'The Cat of Norrhult', a cat behaves in ways that betray a witch's or troll's power behind it, and the cat's strange actions reveal the magic at work in the village. The tale is one of many Swedish stories of animals that are not what they seem.
source: Småland folktale 'The Cat of Norrhult'

name: The Treasure in Säby Creek
description: A hidden treasure said to lie in a creek at Säby in Småland, at the centre of a Swedish folk tale. In the tale 'The Treasure in Säby Creek', the buried hoard is guarded or hard-won, and the treasure-seekers' venture into the creek tests their courage and luck. It belongs to the large Swedish family of tales about treasure guarded in the landscape.
source: Småland folktale 'The Treasure in Säby Creek'

name: The Sea King's Ring
maker: Given by the sea king in the ballad
powers: Binds the maiden to the sea king.
description: A golden ring given by the sea king in the Swedish ballad 'Agneta and the Sea King', a version of the old ballad about the maiden taken by the sea folk. The ring is the gift that binds the maiden to her underwater master; in the ballad's ending the ring and its owner part in sorrow. The ballad is documented in Swedish song collections from the 18th century.
source: Swedish ballad 'Agneta and the Sea King'

name: The Madonna's Golden Shoe
maker: Belonging to the church Madonna statue
description: The golden shoe of the Virgin Mary's statue, at the centre of the Swedish tale 'The Fiddler Who Got the Madonna's Golden Shoe'. In the tale a fiddler who plays for the church is rewarded when the Madonna herself bestows her golden shoe on him. The tale is one of Sweden's many stories of a church statue that comes alive.
source: Swedish folktale 'The Fiddler Who Got the Madonna's Golden Shoe'

name: The Broom King
maker: The broom itself in the tale
powers: Rules all brooms and sweeps away the story's dangers.
description: The broom king, the broom that rules all brooms, from the Swedish tale 'The Broom's Broom King of All Brooms'. In the tale a broom proves to be the king of its kind, sweeping away the story's dangers with a command that no other broom could match. The tale plays on the humble household object raised to kingship.
source: Swedish folktale 'The Broom's Broom King of All Brooms'

name: The Cowbell of the Skogsrå
maker: Worn or carried by the forest spirit
powers: Its tinkling warns of the skogsrå's presence in the woods.
description: A cowbell heard in the forest in Swedish belief, and a mark of the skogsrå, the forest spirit who leads cattle astray. She is said to ring her bell or to ride a cow, and the tinkle of a bell where no cow is to be seen warns of her presence. The cowbell is part of the skogsrå's folklore as a seductive and misleading spirit.
source: Swedish belief about the skogsrå

name: The Luckstone
powers: Brings luck and wards off the mare and misfortune.
description: A luckstone (lyckosten), a stone with a natural hole, worn on a cord or kept in the pocket for luck and protection in Swedish folk tradition. Such pierced stones were also called 'hängesten', hanging stones, or 'örngottsstenar' and were hung in stables, on the neck, or by the bed to ward off the mare and misfortune.
source: Swedish folk belief about pierced amulet stones

name: The Church Keys
material: Iron or brass key and a Bible
maker: Church key, used by the household
powers: Turns or shakes to reveal the name of a thief.
description: The church key used in the Swedish divination called nyckelprövning, the key test. A key was bound between the pages of a Bible, which was then hung or turned while names were read, and it was believed the key would point out or shake at the name of a thief. The key-and-Bible test is documented in Swedish folk tradition for finding stolen goods.
source: Swedish folk tradition of the key-and-Bible test

name: The Black Book of the Clergy
powers: Conjurations and signs for summoning and binding spirits.
description: The black book (svartbok), a manual of black magic that Swedish tradition placed in the hands of a priest or 'klok' man who had studied 'the black art'. Actual svartkonstböcker, filled with conjurations, signs, and instructions, survive in Swedish archives from the 17th-19th centuries; legend said the priest's black book could be passed on only on his deathbed.
source: Swedish svartkonstbok tradition and archives

name: The Votive Ship
powers: A thank-offering that places the ship under the church's protection.
description: The votive ship (votivskepp), a model ship hung from the vault of a Swedish church, given in thanks for rescue at sea. Sailors and fishermen commissioned the models after storms, and hundreds still hang in Swedish churches and chapels. The votive ship joins the church's prayers to the sea's dangers, a documented custom from the late Middle Ages onward.
source: Swedish church votive-ship tradition
